h1: Texting and Cell Phone Ticket Lawyer in El Paso, Texas
intro: El Paso drivers can be ticketed under two different laws for the same phone: the statewide texting ban and the city's hands-free ordinance. For a flat fee from $59, attorney Robert Navar sorts out which one you were cited under and works toward a dismissal or a disposition with no conviction.
summaryHeading: Which law were you cited under: the Texas texting ban or El Paso's hands-free ordinance?
summary: Texas has banned texting while driving statewide since 2017 under Transportation Code 545.4251. It applies to reading, writing or sending electronic messages while the vehicle is moving.

El Paso goes further: the city's hands-free ordinance prohibits holding a phone at all while driving within city limits, which is why many El Paso Police phone tickets are written under the city ordinance rather than the state law.
Real defenses exist: using GPS or navigation, being stopped at a light rather than moving, and the officer's inability to see what was actually on your screen.
Flat fees: $59 in El Paso Municipal Court, $69 in Justice of the Peace, Horizon City, Socorro, San Elizario, Clint and Anthony courts. Hire online in two minutes; you generally do not need to appear.

sections.heading: Two Laws, One Phone: Texas Texting Ban vs. El Paso Hands-Free
paragraphs: The statewide law, Transportation Code 545.4251, took effect in September 2017. It makes it a misdemeanor to use a portable wireless device to read, write or send an electronic message while operating a motor vehicle, unless the vehicle is stopped. It is deliberately narrow: it targets messaging, not every use of a phone, with exceptions for navigation, emergency calls and hands-free operation.

El Paso adopted its own hands-free ordinance before the state acted. Inside the city limits, holding a phone to talk, text or do anything else while driving is a violation on its own. Because the city ordinance is broader and easier to prove, El Paso Police officers often write phone tickets under it, and those cases are heard in El Paso Municipal Court. DPS troopers and Sheriff's deputies enforce the state statute, and their tickets go to a Justice of the Peace precinct.
Which law you were cited under changes the defenses and what the prosecutor has to prove, so it's the first thing we look at. This page is general information, not legal advice about your case.

sections.heading: Where These Tickets Get Written in El Paso
paragraphs: Phone tickets cluster where traffic is slow and officers can see into cars: the long signal cycles on Mesa Street, the stop-and-go on Montana Avenue and Lee Treviño, the Spur 601 and I-10 frontage roads near the Fort Bliss gates at shift change, and the Zaragoza corridor on the East Side. An officer in the next lane or on a motorcycle looks down, sees a lit screen and a hand, and writes the ticket.

What the officer actually saw is usually far less than what the citation implies. From outside the car, an officer can see a glowing screen and a hand near it — not whether you were typing a text, tapping a map, changing a song, or picking up a phone that slid off the seat. Under the state texting law, the prosecutor has to prove the messaging part. Under the city ordinance, the question is whether you were holding and using the device while driving. Either way, the officer's vantage point is the pressure point in negotiation.

sections.heading: Defenses to a Texting or Hands-Free Ticket
paragraphs: These cases have more legitimate defenses than most Class C tickets because the law draws lines the officer can't see from the road. The state texting statute does not apply when the vehicle is stopped, so a driver reading a message at a red light on Zaragoza is not violating 545.4251 — though the city ordinance may still be an issue. Navigation is another carved-out category: following a GPS app is not reading or sending an electronic message.

We ask every client to preserve the phone's own records: screenshots of the messages timeline, navigation history, call log, and any carrier data showing no message was sent or received at the citation time. Prosecutors in El Paso County respond to that kind of proof. We also look at whether the officer's position allowed a clear view and whether the citation names the right ordinance or statute.

list.text: the state texting ban applies only while the vehicle is in motion; a message read at a full stop is outside the statute.
using a mapping app is not sending or reading an electronic message under the state law.
a phone in a dash mount operated by voice or a single tap is generally allowed under both laws.
carrier logs and screenshots showing no activity at the citation time are strong negotiating evidence.
a city ordinance ticket written by a county officer, or vice versa, is a citation defect we raise.

paragraphs: When you hire us online or call 915-503-1600, we file a notice of appearance promptly, so the appearance date stops being a failure-to-appear risk. We identify the charging law, gather the phone evidence described above, and pull the officer's notes.

At the pretrial docket we ask for a dismissal when the evidence supports it, and otherwise for a deferred disposition — a court fee, a clean deferral period, and the case dismissed with no conviction. sections.heading: Fines, Insurance and Why Paying Is the Expensive Choice
paragraphs: A first texting offense under the state law is a fine-only misdemeanor, with the amount set by the court and court costs added; city ordinance tickets are likewise fine-only Class C cases. The fine is rarely the real problem. Paying the ticket is a guilty plea, and a distracted-driving conviction is reported to DPS and visible to your insurer at renewal. A conviction may affect premiums depending on your history, carrier and other rating factors, and distracted-driving convictions are among those carriers watch closely.

Compare that with a flat $59 in Municipal Court or $69 in JP and area courts and a case aimed at ending without a conviction. A second citation from the same stop — speeding, no insurance, or a red light — is added at a discounted rate and resolved on the same docket. Use the free ticket and warrant lookup if you aren't sure where the case is filed.

sections.heading: Screenshots First: What to Preserve and Send Us
paragraphs: Before you do anything else, take screenshots on your phone: the messages app around the citation time, your navigation app's recent trips, and your call log. Don't delete anything. If you were stopped at a light, note the intersection. Write down where the officer was and what they said they saw at the window — that statement matters later.

Then look at the appearance date and don't let it pass. Don't pay it and don't request defensive driving on your own, which can lock in a plea before we've looked at the charge. If the date already went by, there may be a warrant: read our warrant recall page and call us the same day. When you hire us, send the citation (both sides), your driver's license, the screenshots above, and any letter the court has mailed you.

faqs.q: Is it illegal to hold your phone while driving in El Paso?
faqs.a: Inside the El Paso city limits, yes — the hands-free ordinance bars holding a phone while driving, regardless of what you're doing with it. Outside the city, Transportation Code 545.4251 bans reading, writing or sending electronic messages while moving, but does not by itself ban holding a phone.

faqs.q: I was using Google Maps, not texting. Is that a defense?
faqs.a: Under the state texting law, yes — navigation use is not reading or sending an electronic message. Under the city ordinance the question is whether you were holding the phone, so a mounted phone matters. Preserve your navigation history; it is the kind of evidence prosecutors respond to.

faqs.q: I was stopped at a red light when the officer saw me. Does that matter?
faqs.a: It can. The state texting statute applies only while the vehicle is moving, so reading a message at a full stop is outside it. City ordinance tickets are analyzed differently, which is why the first thing we check is which law the officer cited.

faqs.q: Will a texting ticket raise my insurance?
faqs.a: If you pay it and it becomes a conviction, it may, depending on your carrier, your history and other rating factors. A dismissal or deferred disposition keeps the conviction off your DPS record, which is the point of contesting it.

faqs.q: Do I have to go to court for a cell phone ticket?
faqs.a: Generally not when you hire us. We file the appearance, negotiate at the pretrial docket and report the result. Only an uncommon trial setting would require your presence.

faqs.q: Can you handle a texting ticket from a DPS trooper on I-10?
faqs.a: Yes. Trooper tickets are written under the state statute and filed in an El Paso County Justice of the Peace precinct, where our flat fee is $69. We also handle phone tickets in the Horizon City, Socorro, San Elizario, Clint and Anthony courts.
